episode.title: Cariboo Signals - Arts, Culture & Digital Storytelling
episode.description:
Riley and Casey explore technology and society in rural communities. Today's focus: Arts, Culture & Digital Storytelling.

THIS WEEK WE'RE ASKING: Who gets to leave, and who has to stay?

NEWS ROUNDUP: We break down MEET THE CANDIDATES: City councillor candidate Nathan Wiebe and MEET THE CANDIDATES: City councillor candidate Kayla Zaruk, plus 10 more stories, and explore what these developments mean for communities like ours.

RURAL CONNECTIONS: When a talented kid leaves a small town, is that a loss for the town or a success for the kid, and what does the town owe the people who stay? Topics include: Inuit Language Protection Act and language rights in signage and commerce, Archives, lost films and rights ownership in the Iqaluit animation rediscovery, Digital distribution versus gatekeeping by platforms and festivals, Audience measurement and whether small towns should count local viewers rather than exports, Identity, local artists and copyright in cultural products like tattoo designs.

Hosts: Riley (Tech optimist with an engineering background) and Casey (Community-first skeptic of tech promises).

COMMUNITY SPOTLIGHT: Literacy Quesnel Society

discussion.central_question: When a talented kid leaves a small town, is that a loss for the town or a success for the kid, and what does the town owe the people who stay?
discussion.riley_position: Leaving can be a success for the individual and digital tools make distribution possible from anywhere, so a town's creative economy can be built on local institutions, training pipelines, and reach beyond the town.
riley_key_evidence: Nunavut's Department of Culture and Heritage has run a Language Implementation Fund and Inuktut Affairs unit for more than a decade, following a $200,000 addition for Inuktut film, television and digital media in 2013.
In July 2025, Nunavut News reported rediscovered animation by roughly thirteen Inuit filmmakers from about half a century ago, including Aoudla Pudlat, Pitaloosie Saila and Kanayuk Pootoogook.
Nyla Innuksuk, who grew up in Iqaluit, is a director, writer and VR creator and CEO of Mixtape VR, and imagineNATIVE and TIFF have featured Indigenous filmmakers from the circumpolar region.
discussion.casey_position: Export success hides a loss for the town, since the audience and archive can leave with the talent, and the town should measure what its own residents can see and keep rather than what it exports.
casey_key_evidence: The Inuit Language Protection Act's commissioner argues Inuktut advertising pays off, but the department also offers businesses a $5,000 grant to comply, so the market argument has a subsidy underneath it.
The 2013 $200,000 line is small for a film industry, and the article gives no figures on how much reaches filmmakers versus administration or whether training graduates stayed in the field.

Rediscovered Inuit films were lost because nobody kept prints, masters or rights paperwork, making it an archive problem, and small-town counts of local screenings have no funding or institution to hold them long term.
discussion.resolution: They agreed the archive and the audience are the key structural issues and that nobody currently pays to hold a town's film data, and proposed a cheap experiment of one locally screened film per season with a published, method-labelled count. They still disagreed on whether the export is a success, with Riley seeing it as a success for the person who left and Casey seeing a loss nobody can see.

research.block:
PRE-RESEARCHED INSIGHTS FOR THE DEEP DIVE

RESEARCH QUESTION: Does the Iqaluit Inuit creative boom have a real institutional base (language law, funding, training), or is it mainly a story about individual talent and identity?

Findings:
- The NYT piece (dated October 2026 in its URL) describes Iqaluit, Nunavut's capital and the only city in Canada's Arctic, as the setting for writers and artists turning language, land and identity into books, films and tattoos.
- Nunavut has a legal framework that touches creative and commercial work. The Inuit Language Protection Act requires private businesses and government offices across Nunavut to offer services and communications in Inuktitut or Inuinnaqtun, including public signs, posters, advertising and invoices. CBC reported that these provisions came into force on July 9 (the snippet doesn't give the year, which appears to be 2019).
- Public money supports Inuktut in media. In 2013 the Government of Nunavut's Department of Culture and Heritage announced $200,000 in additional funding for Inuktut in film, television and digital media. The department still runs a Language Implementation Fund and an Inuktut Affairs unit that administers language funding.
- Businesses can get a $5,000 grant from the same department to help them comply with the language law. The Nunavut languages commissioner has argued that Inuktut advertising pays off.
- The roots are older than the current wave. In July 2025, Nunavut News reported a "historic discovery" of animation by Inuit filmmakers from roughly half a century ago. Thirteen artists' published films were named, including Aoudla Pudlat, Pitaloosie Saila and Kanayuk Pootoogook, after that work had been effectively lost.
- Training pipelines are emerging. CBC covered a media production program teaching Inuit youth scripting and filmmaking, and the Inuit Broadcasting Corp. launched hands-on training for Inuit youth.
- Festival visibility is growing. imagineNATIVE in Toronto screens Inuit filmmakers, and TIFF has featured circumpolar Indigenous filmmakers.
- Nyla Innuksuk, who grew up in Iqaluit, is a director, writer and VR creator and CEO of Mixtape VR. She is a concrete example of a local kid moving into digital storytelling.

Suggested angle: Riley (optimist) can argue that the Iqaluit story shows digital tools and distribution let a small Arctic community reach global audiences, citing Innuksuk's VR work, the rediscovered 1970s animation now reaching audiences, and youth training programs. Casey (skeptic) can push back that the creative economy here rests heavily on government mandates and grants, such as the language law and the $200,000 film fund, so "identity-driven art" may partly be a policy product rather than a market success. Casey can also ask how much of the audience is local versus festival and institutional, and whether a city of this size can sustain a creative career path without leaving. Both can agree that language protection and storytelling are linked, since the work itself is in Inuktut and carries land and language knowledge. The debate can turn on whether digital distribution helps preserve that language or dilutes it.

Note: I did not run independent searches on the Partake Foods or Mother Jones pieces. The Mother Jones article ("Stop the Steal Never Stopped") is about election politics rather than arts or culture, so it may fit the theme poorly unless the episode frames it around media narratives or documentary storytelling.

ELECTION RESEARCH: 2026 B.C. provincial general election

Background for the roundup's election stories and any race the hosts mention. It is not the deep dive's subject.

Names below come from the roll-call searches and the pages I read. Every claim carries its outlet and date. Where a snippet gave no date, I say so.

---

**FINDINGS: Cariboo-Chilcotin**

*Lorne Doerkson (Conservative, incumbent)*
- Current office: Interim leader of the BC Conservatives and Leader of the Opposition. Wikipedia describes him this way; the Globe and Mail (Sept. 26, 2026) reports he "takes the reins" of the party. (Wikipedia, undated snippet; Globe and Mail, Sept. 26, 2026)
- Earlier election: first elected in Cariboo-Chilcotin in 2020 as a B.C. Liberal, winning 6,600 votes (51.25%) over the NDP's Scott Andrews (32.46%). (Elections BC 2020 Statement of Votes; Vancouver Sun, undated snippet)
- 2024 election: re-elected as a Conservative. He crossed the floor from B.C. United on May 31, 2024. The Conservatives won the riding by 7,722 votes. (Penticton Western News, Oct. 20, 2024; bcballot.ca candidate page, undated)
- Controversy (allegation, reported, not a finding): Doerkson's Sept. 29, 2026 letter to the Insurance Bureau of Canada, the Law Society of BC, the Trial Lawyers Association of BC and the Canadian Bar Association's B.C. branch reportedly committed a Conservative government to overhauling auto insurance, including ending no-fault. MoveUP, the ICBC union, made the letter public. (The Tyee, Oct. 8, 2026, headline and deck only, full text not read; Global News, undated snippet; Daily Hive, undated snippet)
- CBC described the letter as "leaked" and said it proposed a hybrid system that would allow lawsuits again. (CBC News, undated snippet)
- Doerkson's response, as reported: Vaughn Palmer's Vancouver Sun column contrasts Doerkson's "we are working on it" remarks to reporters with the letter's detail. The column date was not visible in the snippet. I did not find a direct Doerkson statement on the letter in the sources I could read.

*Kathryn Askew (BC NDP)*
- Named as the BC NDP candidate for Cariboo-Chilcotin. She is a retired teacher from Canim Lake and a former BCTF local president and bargaining chair. (100 Mile Free Press, Oct. 1, 2026; BC NDP release, Oct. 1, 2026, per search snippet)
- Earlier runs: none found in the sources I searched.
- No controversy found.

*Douglas Gook (BC Green)*
- On the ballot per the Elections BC candidate report and the Canadian Elections Tracker. (Elections BC candidate report; Canadian Elections Tracker, undated)
- 2020: ran as the BC Green candidate in Cariboo North and lost. He received 707 votes (6.38%), finishing fourth behind Coralee Oakes (Liberal, 5,367 votes, 48.42%). (Elections BC 2020 Statement of Votes)
- 2017: ran in Nechako Lakes, receiving about 9% of the vote. (Williams Lake Tribune, undated snippet, referencing the 2017 provincial election)
- No controversy found.

---

**FINDINGS: Prince George-North Cariboo**

*Sheldon Clare (Conservative, incumbent)*
- Office: MLA for Prince George-North Cariboo since 2024. Opposition House Leader per Wikipedia. (Wikipedia, undated snippet)
- 2024: won the seat with 11,430 votes (56.82%), defeating independent Coralee Oakes (21.84%). (Quesnel Cariboo Observer, Oct. 7, 2026)
- Leadership bid: Clare said in January 2026 he was running for the BC Conservative leadership. (Times Colonist/Canadian Press, Jan. 8, 2026) He and MLA Steve Kooner withdrew, per CFJC Kamloops (Feb. 28, 2026).
- Controversy (allegations, not findings): The BC NDP accused Clare of saying municipal politicians "should be hanged," defending residential school death rates, and comparing gun restrictions to the internment of Japanese Canadians. The NDP made this claim in an X post and in a deadline-day statement reported by the Indo-Canadian Voice (undated snippet; the article refers to "deadline day," which I take to mean Oct. 3, 2026). The Western Standard (day 14 of the campaign, undated snippet) reported the same accusations. PressProgress (undated snippet) reported that Clare made the "hanged" remark in a Conservative BC municipal elections chat "last month." I could not read the PressProgress page to confirm the date.
- Clare's response: I did not find a response to the 2026 allegations in the sources I could read. His My Prince George Now interview (Sept. 23, 2026) addresses his leadership-era support for Kerry-Lynn Findlay and his support for Doerkson, not these remarks.

*Denice Bardua (BC NDP)*
- Named as the BC NDP candidate for Prince George-North Cariboo. (CKPG Today, Oct. 3, 2026; Quesnel Cariboo Observer, Oct. 7, 2026)
- 2024: ran for the same party in the same riding and finished third with 17.03%, behind Clare and Oakes. (Quesnel Cariboo Observer, Oct. 7, 2026; Prince George Citizen, undated snippet)
- No controversy found.

*Randy Thompson (BC Green)*
- Named as the BC Green candidate. (BC Greens candidate page; Quesnel Cariboo Observer, Oct. 7, 2026; Prince George Daily News, Oct. 11, 2026)
- 2024: ran as the BC Green candidate in the same riding and received just over 4% of the vote. (Quesnel Cariboo Observer, Oct. 7, 2026; BC Greens candidate page)
- He previously served two years on the BC Green Provincial Council. (BC Greens candidate page, undated)
- No controversy found.

The show has not yet established a full record for every candidate in these races. Kathryn Askew's earlier runs and any controversy involving her are still open questions.

---
